etre-heures.title: "Il est huit heures" — again, no "avoir"... or rather, just "être"!
etre-heures.body: Unlike age (which uses avoir), telling the time in French uses the verb être: il est huit heures (it's eight o'clock). Notice that here the "il" doesn't refer to anyone — it's an impersonal "il", just there to build the sentence, like the "it" in "it's raining" in English.

le-midi-almoco-longo.title: "Le midi" in France is time to sit down and really eat
le-midi-almoco-longo.body: In France, lunch (le déjeuner, from around noon to 1 p.m.) is usually a real break — many restaurants and work canteens serve a full meal (starter, main course, sometimes dessert), and it's common to set aside 45 minutes to an hour just for it, rather than eating quickly at your desk.
